tips.title: Ecosystem includes the non-living
tips.body: A **community** is only the living things; an **ecosystem** is the community **plus** the soil, water, light and temperature. If a definition you write has no mention of non-living parts, it is a community, whatever you called it.

tips.title: If it is alive, it is biotic
tips.body: Competition, predation, disease and food are **biotic** because they involve organisms. Light, temperature, water, pH and wind are **abiotic**. One test settles every example: is it alive, or does it come from something alive?

tips.title: Random for how many, a line for how it changes
tips.body: **Random quadrats** estimate a **population**; a **belt transect** shows how distribution **changes across a gradient**. A transect is deliberately not random, so do not criticise it for that — it is the right tool for a different question.

tips.title: Mean per square metre, then times the area
tips.body: Convert the mean per quadrat to a **density per m²** first — divide by the quadrat area if it is not 1 m² — then multiply by the total area. Doing it in that order makes a 0.25 m² quadrat no harder than a 1 m² one.

tips.title: Name where the 90% went
tips.body: **Respiration as heat**, **egestion**, **excretion**, and **parts not eaten**. Saying *energy is lost* scores nothing on its own; the mark is for where it went, and there are four places.

why.matters:
Nothing in an ecosystem is independent of anything else, and that is not a slogan — it is a prediction. Change one population and others change, often ones that seem unconnected, because they are linked by food, by competition or by something one of them provides.

The rest of the topic is about **measuring** that honestly. You cannot count every organism in a field, so you sample — and how you sample decides whether the number you end up with means anything at all.

examples.title: Why you count a field by throwing a quadrat
examples.body:
Nobody counts every daisy in a meadow. A **quadrat** is placed at **randomly** chosen coordinates, the plants inside it are counted, and the mean per quadrat is scaled up to the whole area.

The randomness is what makes the arithmetic honest. A person choosing where to put the frame will choose interesting-looking patches without meaning to, and the estimate comes out too high. Along a changing environment — up a shore, into a wood — you use a **transect** instead, because there the whole point is that position matters.

examples.title: Why removing one species empties a habitat
examples.body:
Take out a predator and its prey increase, which sounds obvious until you follow it further: the prey then eat out the plants, the plants that supported other animals disappear, and species with no direct connection to the predator vanish.

That is **interdependence**. Organisms depend on each other for food, for shelter, for pollination and for seed dispersal, so a change anywhere propagates. It is also why an answer about an ecosystem should follow a chain rather than name an outcome: each link is a mark, and the end of the chain is often somewhere unexpected.

visual.alt: A flow chart of interdependence: removing a predator lets its prey increase, the prey eat out the plants, and species that depended on those plants lose their habitat

examples.title: Why two similar species rarely share a place
examples.body:
Organisms compete for what is in short supply — plants for light, water, space and mineral ions; animals for food, water, mates and territory. Two species that need exactly the same things are in direct competition, and usually one does better.

That is why an introduced species can be so damaging. The grey squirrel did not attack the red one; it competed with it and carried a disease it was itself resistant to. Nothing dramatic has to happen for a population to disappear — a small, permanent disadvantage is enough.

boxes.title: Same needs
boxes.body: Direct competition, and one usually wins.

boxes.title: Introduced species
boxes.body: Arrives without the things that limited it.

visual.alt: Four boxes round a centre reading what is in short supply: plants competing for light, water, space and minerals, animals for food, water, mates and territory, species with the same needs competing directly, and introduced species arriving without their usual limits

steps.title: Levels of organisation
steps.body:
Ecology has its own ladder of terms, and using the wrong rung is an easy mark to lose. From smallest to largest:

- An **individual** — one organism.
- A **population** — all the organisms of **one species** in a habitat.
- A **community** — all the **populations of all the species** living in a habitat.
- An **ecosystem** — the community **together with the non-living parts** of the habitat, and the interactions between them.

The jump that matters is the last one. A community is **only the living things**; an **ecosystem includes the non-living** — the soil, the water, the light, the temperature. So a pond's community is the fish, plants and insects; the pond **ecosystem** is those plus the water, the mud and the sunlight falling on it.

Two more terms you need:

- A **habitat** is the place an organism lives.
- **Biodiversity** is the variety of different species in an ecosystem.

steps.title: Abiotic and biotic factors
steps.body:
Communities are affected by two kinds of factor, and the names are simply Greek for *without life* and *with life*.

**Abiotic factors — the non-living conditions:**

- light intensity
- temperature
- moisture, or water availability
- soil pH and mineral content
- wind intensity and direction
- carbon dioxide level (for plants) and oxygen level (for aquatic animals)
- **pollutants**, such as sulfur dioxide in the air or excess fertiliser washed into water

**Biotic factors — the effects of other living things:**

- **competition** — for food, water, light, space or mates
- **predation** — being eaten
- **disease** — pathogens spreading through a population
- the **availability of food**
- new species arriving and outcompeting the existing ones

A useful test: if the factor **is alive or comes from something alive**, it is biotic. Food is biotic; water is abiotic. Predators are biotic; temperature is not.

**How competition and predation change a community.** When two species compete for the same limited resource, the one better at getting it increases and the other declines, and it may disappear from that habitat. Predators and prey are linked: when prey are plentiful the predators have more food and increase; more predators eat more prey, so the prey fall; with less food the predators then fall too, and the prey recover. So the two populations rise and fall in turn, with the predators' peak coming a little after the prey's.

A change in one factor rarely affects only one species, because the species are connected — which is the subject of the next step.

steps.title: Interdependence, mutualism and parasitism
steps.body:
**Interdependence** means the species in a community **depend on one another** — for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal and more. Because of it, a change affecting one species can ripple through the whole community.

If a population of insects falls, the birds that eat them have less food, so the bird population falls too; the plants those insects pollinated set fewer seeds. Nothing in a community is affected alone.

Two particular relationships are named on the specification.

**Mutualism** — a relationship where **both** species benefit:

- **Oxpeckers** and large mammals: the bird eats ticks and parasites from the mammal's skin. The bird gets food; the mammal is cleaned.
- **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria** in the **root nodules of legumes**: the bacteria get sugars and a place to live; the plant gets nitrogen compounds.
- **Cleaner fish** and larger fish: the same arrangement, underwater.
- **Chemosynthetic bacteria** in **giant tube worms**: the bacteria get shelter and raw materials; the worm gets food.

**Parasitism** — one species, the **parasite**, **benefits while the other, the host, is harmed**:

- **fleas** on a mammal, feeding on its blood
- **head lice** on a human
- **tapeworms** in an intestine, absorbing digested food
- **mistletoe** on a tree, taking water and minerals

The distinction is simply **who benefits**: both, or only one at the other's expense.

steps.title: Quadrats and transects: estimating a population
steps.body:
**Core practical 9.5** asks you to investigate the relationship between organisms and their environment using **quadrats** and **belt transects**, and 9.6 asks you to work out numbers from the data.

**A quadrat** is a square frame of known area, placed on the ground, in which you count the organisms or estimate the percentage cover. Quadrats must be placed **randomly** if you are estimating a population — using random number pairs as coordinates on a grid — because choosing where to put them would bias the result towards the places you noticed the species.

**A belt transect** is a line across a habitat, along which quadrats are placed at regular intervals. This is **not** random, and deliberately so: a transect is used when you want to see how a species **changes across a gradient** — up a beach, or from a hedge into a field.

So the two techniques answer different questions: **quadrats placed randomly** estimate *how many*; a **transect** shows *how the distribution changes*. The next step works through the practical itself.

steps.title: Core practical 9.5: a belt transect from shade into the open
steps.body:
**Core practical 9.5** asks you to investigate the relationship between organisms and their environment. The specification's method is a **belt transect along a gradient**, for example from deep shade under a tree out into open grass, where light changes a great deal over a few metres.

**Method.**

1. Lay a **tape measure** in a straight line from the shaded area into the open.
2. Place a **quadrat**, for example 0.25 m², at **regular intervals** along the tape, say every 2 m, always on the same side of it.
3. At each quadrat, measure the abiotic factor: **light intensity** with a **light meter** held just above the plants. Soil moisture or temperature can be measured the same way.
4. In each quadrat, **count** the plants of the species you are studying, or **estimate its percentage cover** where single plants cannot be told apart, as with grass or moss. Use an **identification key** to be sure which species is which.
5. **Repeat** the transect along one or two parallel lines, and find the mean at each distance.
6. Plot the number or percentage cover, and the light intensity, against distance along the transect, and look for a pattern.

**Variables.** The **independent** variable is the position along the transect, and with it the light intensity. The **dependent** variable is the number or percentage cover of the species. **Control** variables: the same quadrat size, the same interval, readings taken at about the same time of day in the same weather, and the same person estimating cover.

**Sources of error.**

- Percentage cover is a **judgement**, so two people can give different values.
- A species can be **misidentified**.
- **Light** changes as clouds pass, so readings taken minutes apart may not be comparable.
- A pattern that follows light does not prove light is the cause: soil moisture also changes between the shade of a tree and open ground.

**Safety.** Wash your hands after handling soil and plants, watch for stinging plants and uneven ground, and stay away from water and roads unless supervised.

steps.title: Energy through a food chain
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* This section covers spec points 9.7B and 9.8B.

At each step of a food chain, **only about 10% of the energy** is passed on to the next level. The rest is **transferred to less useful forms**, and you should be able to say where it goes:

- **respiration**, which releases energy as **heat** to the surroundings
- **egestion** — the parts that are not digested, lost in faeces
- **excretion** — waste such as urine
- parts that are **not eaten**, such as bones, roots or bark

Because each level receives less energy than the one below, it can support **less biomass**, and usually **fewer organisms**. That is also why food chains are short: after four or five levels there is too little energy left to support another.

steps.title: Pyramids of biomass, and percentage biomass
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* **Biomass** is the mass of living material, usually given as dry mass per square metre. Draw each trophic level as a bar whose width is its biomass, producers at the bottom, and the result is a **pyramid of biomass**.

It narrows going up for the same reason food chains are short: each level receives only a small fraction of the energy of the one below, so it can build only a small fraction of the biomass.

Counting organisms can mislead, because one oak tree can feed thousands of caterpillars, so a pyramid of **numbers** can be wider in the middle than at the base. Biomass takes the size of each organism into account, which is why the pyramid of **biomass** keeps its shape.

The **percentage of biomass passed on** is worked out the same way as energy efficiency:

$\text{percentage passed on} = \dfrac{\text{biomass at the higher level}}{\text{biomass at the level below}} \times 100$

visuals.problem: The producers in a field have a biomass of 1200 g/m² and the primary consumers 96 g/m². What percentage of the biomass is passed on?

steps.title: Human effects: fish farms, introduced species and eutrophication
steps.body:
Spec point 9.9 names three human interactions, and each can help or harm **biodiversity**.

**Fish farming.** Fish are reared in cages or pens, often in lakes or sea lochs.

- *Positive:* it supplies fish **without depleting wild stocks**, which gives overfished species a chance to recover.
- *Negative:* waste and uneaten food enrich the water and can cause **eutrophication**; **disease and parasites** spread from crowded farmed fish to wild fish; and escaped fish compete with wild ones.

**Introducing non-indigenous species.** A species brought from somewhere else may have **no natural predators or diseases** here, so its population grows and it **outcompetes native species** for food and space. The grey squirrel, brought from North America, has replaced the native red squirrel across most of England and Wales. Some introductions are deliberate and useful, such as a predator brought in as **biological control** of a pest, but they can go wrong if it eats more than its target.

**Eutrophication.** When fertiliser or sewage washes into a lake or river, the extra nitrates and phosphates start a chain:

1. **Algae** grow rapidly on the surface.
2. They **block the light**, so plants below cannot photosynthesise and **die**.
3. **Decomposers** multiply, breaking down the dead plants and algae.
4. Their **respiration uses up the dissolved oxygen**.
5. **Fish and other animals die** for lack of oxygen.

Each link is part of the explanation; *the fertiliser poisons the fish* is not one of them.

**Conservation and reforestation** (9.10) push the other way. Conservation schemes, such as protected areas and breeding programmes, keep endangered species and the species that depend on them. **Reforestation**, planting trees where forest was lost, restores habitats so biodiversity can recover, and the growing trees remove **carbon dioxide** by photosynthesis.

visuals.alt: A table of the eutrophication sequence: nitrates wash in, algae grow fast, light is blocked, plants below die, decomposers multiply, the oxygen is used up, and fish die

steps.title: Going deeper: humans, biodiversity and food security
steps.body:
**Human interactions, positive and negative.** Spec point 9.9 asks for both, and a good answer gives some of each rather than a list of harms.

*Negative:* **deforestation** removes habitats and reduces biodiversity; **pollution** from farming and industry poisons water and air, and fertiliser or fish-farm waste causes **eutrophication**; **building** destroys and fragments habitats; **overfishing** removes species faster than they can reproduce; **introducing non-indigenous species** that outcompete the natives.

*Positive:* **conservation schemes** and **nature reserves**; **reforestation** and replanting hedgerows; **fish farming**, which supplies fish without depleting wild stocks; **captive breeding** programmes for endangered species; **recycling** to reduce the demand for raw materials; **fishing quotas** so stocks recover.

**Why biodiversity matters** (9.10). Not for its own sake, but for what depends on it:

- A community with **more species** is **more stable**, because if one species declines others can fill its role. A community of few species can collapse when one fails.
- Species provide **resources** — food, medicines, materials — including ones not yet discovered.
- Ecosystems provide **services** that would be costly to replace: pollination of crops, decomposition, water cycling, and removal of carbon dioxide.

*(Biology only.)* **Food security** (9.11B) means having enough safe food for a population. The specification names these **biological** factors:

- **rising human population**, so more mouths
- **more animal farming**, as wealthier populations eat more meat **and fish**; meat needs far more land and energy per kilojoule because of the 10% rule
- **new pests and pathogens** damaging crops and livestock
- **environmental change caused by human activity**, such as climate change shifting rainfall and where crops can grow
- **sustainability**: land used to grow crops for **biofuels** is not used to grow food, and some farming methods damage the soil they depend on
- the **cost** of agricultural inputs, such as fertiliser, animal feed and fuel

The meat point is the one to be able to explain rather than state: feeding grain to an animal and then eating the animal adds a trophic level, and **90% of the energy is lost** at it. Eating the grain directly feeds far more people from the same land.

*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* **Indicator species** (9.16B) are species whose presence or absence indicates pollution, and using them is worth **evaluating** rather than just describing.

- **Lichens** are sensitive to **sulfur dioxide** in air: many lichen species means clean air, few means polluted.
- **Freshwater shrimps** and **stonefly** nymphs need clean, well-oxygenated water; **bloodworms** and **sludgeworms** survive in **polluted** water.
- For air, as well as lichens, **blackspot fungus on roses** is sensitive to sulfur dioxide, so roses free of blackspot can indicate polluted air.

*For:* cheap, needs no equipment, and shows the **effect over time** rather than at one instant. *Against:* it is **qualitative** rather than precise; a species may be absent for another reason entirely, such as the wrong habitat; and it does not identify **which** pollutant. So indicator species are good for a first survey and poor for a legal measurement — which is the judgement a top answer reaches.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Population**: one species. **Community**: all the species. **Ecosystem**: the community **plus the non-living parts**.
- **Abiotic** factors are non-living — light, temperature, water, pH, wind, pollutants. **Biotic** factors involve other organisms — competition, predation, disease, food.
- **Interdependence**: species depend on one another, so a change to one ripples through the community.
- **Mutualism**: **both** benefit — oxpeckers, cleaner fish, nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules.
- **Parasitism**: the parasite benefits and the **host is harmed** — fleas, head lice, tapeworms, mistletoe.
- **Quadrats** are placed **randomly** to estimate a population; a **belt transect** follows a line to show how distribution **changes**.
- Population estimate = **mean per quadrat × total area ÷ quadrat area**.
- **Core practical 9.5**: a **belt transect** from shade into the open, with a **light meter** at each quadrat; keep the quadrat size and the time of day the same.
- **Biology only**: about **10%** of energy passes to the next trophic level.
- The rest goes to **respiration as heat**, **egestion**, **excretion**, and parts **not eaten**.
- $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{energy transferred}}{\text{energy available}} \times 100$.
- Food chains are **short** because so little energy is left after a few steps.
- Less energy at each level means less **biomass**, so a **pyramid of biomass** narrows going up. Percentage passed on = higher level ÷ level below × 100.
- **Human effects**: **fish farming** spares wild stocks, but its waste can cause **eutrophication**; **non-indigenous species** can outcompete natives; **reforestation** restores habitats and removes CO₂.
- **Eutrophication**: algae grow, block the light, plants die, decomposers use up the oxygen, fish die.
- **Biodiversity** makes a community more **stable**, and provides resources and services.
- **Food security** is affected by population growth, more meat and fish in diets, pests, environmental change caused by humans, sustainability (such as land used for **biofuels**) and cost.
- **Indicator species**: **lichens** and **blackspot fungus on roses** for air; **freshwater shrimps** and **stonefly** for clean water, **bloodworms** and **sludgeworms** for polluted. Cheap and long-term, but qualitative and not specific.

options: Showing how distribution changes across a habitat

questions.prompt: Roughly how much energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
questions.solution: About **10%**. The other 90% goes to respiration as heat, egestion, excretion, and parts not eaten.

questions.prompt: Why is biodiversity important?
questions.solution: With **more species**, others can fill the role of one that declines. Biodiversity also provides resources and services such as pollination.
options: A community with more species is more stable
It increases the number of predators

questions.prompt: A trophic level contains 1000 kJ and the next contains 80 kJ. What is the efficiency, as a percentage?
Where does most of the energy go that is not passed to the next trophic level?
questions.solution: All four routes matter, and naming them is usually a separate mark from the calculation.
options: Respiration as heat, egestion, excretion and parts not eaten

questions.prompt: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five levels?
questions.solution: With about 10% passing on each time, three transfers, across four levels, leave only a **thousandth** of the original energy — not enough to support another level.
options: Too little energy is left to support another level

questions.prompt: Why does producing meat need more land than growing crops for people to eat?
questions.solution: Feeding grain to an animal and eating the animal adds a **trophic level**, and about **90%** of the energy is lost at it.
options: It adds a trophic level, losing about 90% of the energy

questions.prompt: Lichens are used as indicator species for what?
questions.solution: Lichens are sensitive to **sulfur dioxide**: many species means clean air, few means polluted. **Freshwater shrimps** and **stonefly** indicate clean water.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of using indicator species to measure pollution?
questions.solution: It shows that pollution is present but not **how much** or **which pollutant** — and a species may be absent for some other reason entirely.
options: It is qualitative and does not say which pollutant

questions.prompt: A student estimates the number of dandelions in a 2000 m² field. They place ten 1 m² quadrats and count 4, 7, 5, 8, 6, 6, 5, 7, 4 and 8 plants. Calculate the estimated population, explain why the quadrats were placed randomly, and suggest how the estimate could be made more reliable.
questions.solution: The total number of dandelions counted across the ten quadrats is sixty. Dividing this by the ten quadrats gives a mean of six dandelions per quadrat. Since each quadrat has an area of one square metre, this is a density of six dandelions per square metre. Multiplying this density by the total area of two thousand square metres gives an estimated population of twelve thousand dandelions. The quadrats have to be placed randomly, for example by using pairs of random numbers as coordinates on a grid laid over the field, because if the student chose where to put them they would be likely to place them where they had already noticed dandelions growing, which would bias the estimate and make it too high. The estimate could be made more reliable by using a larger number of quadrats, because the mean is then less affected by any one unusually high or low square, and by making sure the quadrats are spread across the whole field rather than concentrated in one part of it.

multiplies by the area to give 12000
explains that random placement avoids bias
describes how randomness is achieved, such as random coordinates
suggests more quadrats and says why that helps

criteria.text: Explains that random placement avoids bias
Describes how the placement is randomised
Suggests using more quadrats, with a reason

questions.modelAnswer:
**The calculation.**

- Total: $4+7+5+8+6+6+5+7+4+8 = 60$
- Mean per quadrat: $60 \div 10 = 6$
- Each quadrat is 1 m², so the density is **6 per m²**
- Estimated population: $6 \times 2000 = \mathbf{12\,000}$ dandelions

Say **estimated**. It is a sample scaled up, not a count.

**Why randomly?** If the student chose where to place them, they would tend to pick spots where they had already **noticed** dandelions, biasing the estimate upwards. Randomness is achieved by laying a grid over the field and using **pairs of random numbers as coordinates**.

**Making it more reliable.** Use **more quadrats**: the mean is then less affected by any one unusually high or low square. Also make sure they are spread across the **whole** field rather than concentrated in one part.

Note that *more reliable* is about **repeatability**, which is why the answer is *more quadrats* rather than *count more carefully*.

questions.prompt: Explain why only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next, and explain what this means for the length of food chains and for the land needed to produce meat.
questions.solution: At each trophic level, only a small proportion of the energy taken in by an organism ends up stored in its body where it can be passed on when it is eaten. Much of the energy is used in respiration, which releases it as heat to the surroundings. Some is lost through egestion, because not all of the food eaten can be digested and the remainder is lost in faeces. Some is lost through excretion, in waste such as urine. In addition, parts of an organism such as bones, roots or bark are often not eaten at all, so the energy in them is never transferred. Taken together these losses mean that only about ten per cent of the energy is passed on. This explains why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels, because after a few steps so little of the original energy remains that it cannot support another level. It also explains why producing meat requires more land than growing crops for people to eat directly, because feeding grain to an animal and then eating that animal adds an extra trophic level, at which about ninety per cent of the energy is lost, so far fewer people can be fed from the same area of land.

energy is lost in egestion as undigested material
energy is lost in excretion, or in parts not eaten
so only about 10% is passed on
food chains are short because too little energy remains
meat needs more land because it adds a trophic level

criteria.text: States that respiration releases energy as heat
States that energy is lost in egestion
States that energy is lost in excretion or in parts not eaten
States that about 10% is passed on
Explains why food chains are short
Explains why meat needs more land

questions.modelAnswer:
**Where the energy goes.** At each level, only a small part of what an organism takes in is stored in its body where it can be passed on:

- **Respiration** releases energy as **heat** to the surroundings.
- **Egestion**: not all food can be digested, and the rest is lost in **faeces**.
- **Excretion**: waste such as **urine** carries energy away.
- **Parts not eaten**: bones, roots and bark are often left.

Together these leave about **10%** to pass on.

**Why food chains are short.** Three transfers of 10% take 10 000 kJ to 1000, then 100, then 10 — a **thousandth** of the original, across four levels. There is simply not enough left to support another level.

**Why meat needs more land.** Feeding grain to an animal and then eating the animal adds an **extra trophic level**, at which about **90%** of the energy is lost. Eating the grain directly feeds far more people from the same area.

The last point is the one worth being able to derive rather than recall: it follows from the 10% rule, and a question about food security is usually testing whether you can make that connection.

questions.prompt: A student places 20 quadrats, each 0.25 m², at random in a meadow of 1500 m². The total number of buttercups counted in all 20 quadrats is 90. Estimate the number of buttercups in the meadow.
questions.solution: Mean per quadrat $= 90 \div 20 = 4.5$. Each quadrat is only $0.25$ m², so the density is $4.5 \div 0.25 = 18$ per m². Estimated population $= 18 \times 1500 = 27\,000$ buttercups.

markScheme.description: divides by 0.25 to get 18 per square metre

questions.prompt: A pyramid of biomass has producers of 2500 g/m², primary consumers of 175 g/m² and secondary consumers of 14 g/m². What percentage of the producers' biomass is present in the secondary consumers?
questions.solution: $\dfrac{14}{2500} \times 100 = 0.56\%$. Checking level by level: $\dfrac{175}{2500} \times 100 = 7\%$, then $\dfrac{14}{175} \times 100 = 8\%$, and $0.07 \times 0.08 = 0.0056$, which is $0.56\%$.

markScheme.description: divides 14 by 2500, or multiplies the two level percentages

questions.prompt: Excess fertiliser washes from a field into a lake. Put the events that follow in order.
questions.solution: Algae grow, block the light, the plants below die, **decomposers** multiply on the dead material, and their **respiration uses up the oxygen**, so the fish die. The fertiliser never poisons the fish directly.

markScheme.description: algae growth before plants die, and decomposers before oxygen falls

items: Algae grow rapidly on the surface
Light is blocked, so plants below die
Decomposers multiply on the dead plants
Respiration by decomposers uses up the oxygen
Fish die for lack of oxygen

questions.prompt: Which is a harmful effect of fish farming on the surrounding ecosystem?
questions.solution: Waste and uneaten food enrich the water, so algae grow and **eutrophication** follows; disease and parasites can also spread to wild fish. On the positive side, farmed fish reduce the pressure on **wild stocks** rather than removing them.

markScheme.description: waste and uneaten food cause eutrophication

options: It removes all the wild fish from the sea
It raises the oxygen level in nearby water
Waste and uneaten food cause eutrophication
It stops wild fish from breeding anywhere

questions.prompt: A belt transect runs from deep shade under a tree into open grass. In each quadrat a student measures light intensity and estimates the percentage cover of moss. Moss cover falls steadily as light intensity rises. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.solution: The data show a **negative correlation**: moss cover falls as light rises. A correlation alone does not show that light is the cause, because soil moisture also changes between the shade of a tree and open grass. Saying there is no link contradicts the data, and saying light kills moss claims a cause the data cannot show.

markScheme.description: a correlation, but another factor may be the cause

options: Bright light kills moss, so none grows in open ground
Moss grows best where light intensity is highest
There is no link between light and moss cover
Moss falls as light rises, but another factor may cause it

questions.prompt: Which of these is a sustainability issue that reduces food security?
questions.solution: Land used to grow crops for **biofuels** is not used to grow food. Eating less meat frees land rather than using more, cheaper inputs make food easier to grow, and a shrinking population needs less food, not more.

markScheme.description: land used for biofuels is not used for food

options: Land used for biofuel crops cannot grow food
Eating less meat means more land is needed
Cheaper fertiliser makes food harder to grow
A shrinking population needs more food

examTechnique.body:
Use the right word for the level of organisation. Population, community and ecosystem are not interchangeable.

For a quadrat calculation, find the mean per quadrat, convert to a density per square metre, then multiply by the total area. Show each step.

Call the result an estimate, and if asked how to improve it say more quadrats, spread across the whole area.

For energy transfer, give the equation, then name where the lost energy went. There are four routes and they carry marks.

When asked about human effects on ecosystems, give positive as well as negative examples. The specification asks for both.

When asked to evaluate indicator species, give what they are good for and what they cannot tell you.
examinerErrors: Defining an ecosystem as all the living things, which is a community.
Calling food or predation an abiotic factor.
Forgetting to divide by the quadrat area when it is not one square metre.
Saying energy is lost without naming where it goes.
Saying energy is destroyed, rather than transferred to less useful forms.
Saying mutualism is where one organism benefits.
Criticising a transect for not being random, when it is not meant to be.
Listing only harmful human effects when the question asks about interactions.
Saying fertiliser in a lake poisons the fish, rather than following the chain through algae and decomposers to the lost oxygen.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer keeps the levels of organisation straight and never uses ecosystem where community is meant. In a sampling calculation it converts to a density per square metre before scaling, so a quadrat that is not one square metre causes no trouble. It names all four routes by which energy is lost, and can then derive both the shortness of food chains and the land cost of meat from the 10% figure rather than recalling them as separate facts. Asked to evaluate indicator species, it gives the cost and time advantages, the qualitative limitation, and a judgement about when each matters.
